title: ANIME WORKOUTS - Would Sekibayashi's Pro Wrestling training from Kengan Ashura work
summary: NH reviews Sekibayashi's pro wrestling regimen from Kengan Ashura (10,000 Hindu squats, 200 rope climbs, one hour of neck bridges, 3x1000 push-ups). It is absurd and not recommended for hypertrophy, but its real lesson is tenacity, daily discipline and surrendering to the craft: anyone can change.
claims: His goal in lifting is not athleticism or strength but to become a beast, a wall of muscle with as much lean mass as possible
Athletes' training is sport-specific; pro wrestlers differ because their body is also a cosmetic artifact to entertain, so they are buff
Spirit is 50% of training; the drive to start often comes from humiliation, helplessness or pressure to evolve
A 6 ft 5 natural focused on hypertrophy could realistically weigh about 280 lb tops while lean; Sekibayashi's 311 lb shredded is fiction
Taller lifters often reach their prime in their late 30s because they have more frame to fill out

Sekibayashi's routine (10,000 Hindu squats, 200 reps of 5 m rope climbs, one hour neck bridge, 3 sets of 1000 push-ups) is ridiculous: no novice could handle or repeat it, and anyone who could would be too strong for it to challenge the baseline
If doable, push-ups would grow delts, chest and triceps, rope climbs biceps, forearms and upper back, neck bridges the neck, while bodyweight squats would not grow the legs much
Pro wrestling training aims first at tenacity: cardiovascular and muscular endurance and the mind's capacity to endure punishment
For pure hypertrophy he cannot recommend such training; his backyard calisthenics routine is a better realistic option
Experiencing hardship early can be discouraging, but those who survive the first years of suck stay in the game more easily
Training every day, while not the most optimal for muscle, builds unbreakable discipline by making lifting part of your schedule like lunch or sleep
Accepting that you will work on your body for the rest of your life is the life-altering realization that creates greatness
What you do in training matters less than doing it and surrendering to the craft even if not optimal; anyone can change
